conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states in its conclusion that the claim is supported by randomized-trial evidence, specifically citing a trial comparing chlorhexidine-alcohol to iodine-alcohol that found a statistically significant reduction in surgical-site infections.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported by randomized-trial evidence, so the view that it is false is not well supported.

The strongest direct evidence is a single-center randomized controlled trial (1,147 participants) comparing chlorhexidine–alcohol with iodine–alcohol before cesarean delivery. Surgical-site infection occurred in 4.0% versus 7.3%, respectively (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90; P=.02): an absolute reduction of 3.3 percentage points. The trial’s outcome included superficial and deep SSI within 30 days.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

There is, however, a reasonable basis for *caution about how definitive or universal* the claim is. Another randomized trial comparing povidone–iodine, chlorhexidine–alcohol, and sequential use found very similar SSI rates (4.6%, 4.5%, and 3.9%; P=.85), concluding that it did not support one particular preparation. This comparison may not precisely match iodine–alcohol, which matters because alcohol itself contributes antiseptic activity.  
https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/abstract/10.1097/aog.0000000000001118~skin-preparation-for-prevention-of-surgical-site-infection?redirectionsource=fulltextview

A 2024 network meta-analysis likewise reported overlapping credible intervals among interventions, although alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of preventing SSI, followed by alcohol-based povidone–iodine.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282

Thus, the precise direct comparison favors chlorhexidine–alcohol, but the total evidence does not establish that it is invariably superior in every cesarean setting or versus every iodine formulation.
